newsitem.title: UK: European energy swaps market banks on deregulation.
newsitem.headline: European energy swaps market banks on deregulation.

text.p: Growth in the European energy swaps market will come from the natural gas and electricity sectors and will hinge on deregulation and successful futures contracts, industry sources said on Monday.
European Union directives and efforts by individual members to liberalize markets should boost local cash markets and indirectly the swaps market.
"I think the energy derivatives market will develop along with liberalization in specific countries," said Jay Fitzgerald, vice-president at Enron Capital and Trade Resources.

Growth in the futures market, including the new IPE natural gas contract launched at the end of January, will complement the cash and derivatives market and not be a competitor, he told a swaps conference.
"The markets are very, very complimentary," Fitzgerald said. "Much of the volume traded in the over the counter market finds its way into the exchange-traded market as a warehouse for risk."

The swaps market continues to attract commercial players, such as refineries, airlines, and metals and paper companies to guard against market volatility in increasingly competitive environments and a proliferation of financial service products.
For the U.K. cash natural gas market, success of the new futures contract would quicken an already fast-developing spot market, said Mahul Raval, a broker at PVM Oil Futures limited.

"The futures market will help the gas market overall ," he told the conference. "I think without it the gas market will still develop, it's just that the futures contract might accelerate it and it might help decelerate it, depending on how it goes."

He said the start of the new futures contract was "quite disappointing" with about only six or so active traders. He expected close to 20 trading participants in the next few weeks, which should help the contract take off.

Although very few derivatives transactions are taking place in the gas market, extremely volatile and seasonal prices and the planned pipeline from Britain to Europe later this decade will eventually help the cash and swaps markets, Raval said.
"Volatility will lead to a floating price system and more sphisticated price risk management including use of derivatives," he said.
